blocks.content: Think about the last time you joined a new company and got your laptop set up.

IT didn't sit down and individually grant you access to the codebase, the deploy dashboard, the HR system, and forty other tools one by one. They picked a role, something like "Backend Engineer", and you instantly had everything a backend engineer needs.
That role based thinking is exactly what RBAC is, and it is one of the most common patterns you will be asked about in system design interviews the moment multiple user types show up.
1. Introduction

RBAC stands for Role Based Access Control. It's a way of deciding who can do what inside a system by grouping permissions into named roles and assigning users to those roles, instead of handing out permissions one at a time.

Almost every system with more than one type of user needs some version of this: a project tool has admins and viewers, a bank app has tellers and auditors, a cloud platform has owners and read only guests.
1.1 The problem without RBAC
Imagine a company with 500 employees and a system that has 40 individual permissions like create_invoice, delete_user, view_salary, export_report, and so on.
Without roles, every single employee gets permissions assigned to them directly, one at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365404-420576125.png
blocks.alt: Users each holding a scattered, different set of individual permissions with no grouping

blocks.content: ["You end up with thousands of individual user to permission mappings that nobody fully remembers.","When someone asks \"why does this person have access to delete invoices\", nobody has a clean answer.","Auditing who can do what becomes a spreadsheet nightmare instead of a quick lookup.","Every new hire needs a human to manually pick the right 15 to 20 permissions, and mistakes creep in."]
items: You end up with thousands of individual user to permission mappings that nobody fully remembers.
When someone asks "why does this person have access to delete invoices", nobody has a clean answer.
Auditing who can do what becomes a spreadsheet nightmare instead of a quick lookup.
Every new hire needs a human to manually pick the right 15 to 20 permissions, and mistakes creep in.

blocks.title: The real cost
blocks.content: It's not the initial setup that hurts, it's six months later when three people have left, five have changed teams, and nobody can say with confidence who can actually touch production data.
2. The core idea
RBAC adds one layer of indirection between users and permissions: the role.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365405-35894430.png
blocks.alt: Users assigned to roles, roles holding permissions, arrow flow

blocks.content: Instead of asking "what can this specific person do", you ask "what role is this person in, and what does that role allow".
2.1 Roles as bundles

A role is just a named bundle of permissions. Admin, Editor, and Viewer are common examples, but roles can be anything that matches how your organization actually works: Support Agent, Billing Manager, Read Only Auditor.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365405-542631854.png
blocks.alt: One Editor role bundling three separate permissions together

blocks.content: Once the Editor role is defined as "can edit posts, can delete comments, can upload media", giving someone that role gives them all three at once. Managing access now means managing role membership, not managing a giant list of individual grants.
2.2 Why this scales operationally
This is the real payoff, and it shows up the moment your user base grows past a handful of people.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365406-740991502.png
blocks.alt: New hire onboarded with a single role assignment step

blocks.content: Compare that to the alternative.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365406-416852518.png
blocks.alt: New hire needing twenty separate manual permission grants, shown as an overloaded red path

blocks.content: {"headers":["Without roles","With RBAC"],"rows":[["Onboarding = 20 manual permission grants","Onboarding = assign 1 role"],["Offboarding = hunt down every grant to remove","Offboarding = remove 1 role"],["Auditing = read every user row","Auditing = read the role definition once"],["Changing a policy = edit every affected user","Changing a policy = edit the role, everyone updates"]]}

blocks.title: Offboarding is where this really matters
blocks.content: When someone leaves and their access isn't fully revoked, that's a security incident waiting to happen. One role removal is much harder to get wrong than remembering fifteen individual permissions.
3. The RBAC model: users, roles, permissions
blocks.text: 3. The RBAC model: users, roles, permissions

blocks.content: RBAC has three core entities and the relationships between them matter as much as the entities themselves.

["User a person or service account that needs to do things in the system.","Role a named collection of permissions, like Admin or Editor.","Permission a single allowed action, like edit_post or delete_user."]
items: User a person or service account that needs to do things in the system.
Role a named collection of permissions, like Admin or Editor.
Permission a single allowed action, like edit_post or delete_user.

blocks.content: 3.1 The many to many relationships
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365407-10746221.png
blocks.alt: A user in a role, that role holding two separate permissions

blocks.content: ["A user can hold multiple roles at once. Someone can be both a Billing Manager and a Support Agent.","A role can hold multiple permissions. Editor bundles edit, comment, and upload rights together.","A permission can belong to multiple roles. Both Admin and Editor might include edit_post."]
items: A user can hold multiple roles at once. Someone can be both a Billing Manager and a Support Agent.
A role can hold multiple permissions. Editor bundles edit, comment, and upload rights together.
A permission can belong to multiple roles. Both Admin and Editor might include edit_post.

blocks.content: This is why RBAC is modeled as two many to many relationships in a database: users to roles, and roles to permissions. Neither side is a simple one to one mapping.
4. Role hierarchies
In most real systems, roles are not flat and unrelated. A senior role usually needs everything a junior role has, plus a bit more.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365408-504256596.png
blocks.alt: Admin role inheriting Editor permissions, which inherits Viewer permissions

blocks.content: Instead of copy pasting the Viewer permission list into the Editor role definition, and then copy pasting the Editor list into Admin, you let each role inherit from the one below it.

["Viewer can read tasks and comments.","Editor inherits everything Viewer has, plus can create and edit tasks.","Admin inherits everything Editor has, plus can delete the project and manage members."]
items: Viewer can read tasks and comments.
Editor inherits everything Viewer has, plus can create and edit tasks.
Admin inherits everything Editor has, plus can delete the project and manage members.

blocks.title: Watch for hierarchy sprawl
blocks.content: Hierarchies are great for two or three levels. Once you have six levels of roles inheriting from each other, tracing what a role actually grants gets just as confusing as the direct grant mess RBAC was meant to fix. Keep hierarchies shallow.
5. RBAC versus ABAC
RBAC decides access purely based on your role. It doesn't care what time it is, whether you own the resource, or which department you're in, just whether your role includes the needed permission.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396365408-311114406.png
blocks.alt: RBAC as simple and static next to ABAC as flexible and dynamic

blocks.content: ABAC, Attribute Based Access Control, takes a more dynamic approach. Access decisions can depend on attributes like time of day, the department the user belongs to, whether the user owns the specific resource, or even the current risk level of the request.

{"headers":["RBAC","ABAC"],"rows":[["Access tied to a fixed role","Access tied to dynamic attributes"],["Simple to reason about and audit","Flexible but harder to trace and debug"],["Good fit for most enterprise apps","Good fit for fine grained, context sensitive rules"],["\"Are you an Editor?\"","\"Are you the owner, during business hours, from a trusted network?\""]]}

You don't need to go deep on ABAC for most interviews. Just know it exists as the more flexible, more complex alternative, and that plenty of real systems use RBAC for the coarse grained access and layer in a few ABAC style checks for specific edge cases like resource ownership.
6. The principle of least privilege
Underneath all of RBAC sits one guiding philosophy: give roles the minimum permissions they actually need, not broad access just in case it might be useful someday.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366500-947856939.png
blocks.alt: Broad access being trimmed down to the minimum needed permissions

blocks.content: It's tempting to make everyone an Admin because it avoids the annoyance of permission errors. That convenience is exactly how a support intern ends up able to delete production databases.

["Design roles around what a job actually requires, not around what would be convenient to have.","A Support Agent role should probably read tickets and issue refunds, not delete user accounts.","Review roles periodically. Permissions added for a one off task have a habit of never getting removed."]
items: Design roles around what a job actually requires, not around what would be convenient to have.
A Support Agent role should probably read tickets and issue refunds, not delete user accounts.
Review roles periodically. Permissions added for a one off task have a habit of never getting removed.

blocks.title: Least privilege is not paranoia
blocks.content: It's just recognizing that every extra permission is one more way something can go wrong, whether through a mistake, a compromised account, or an insider threat.
7. Where RBAC shows up in the real world
blocks.text: 7. Where RBAC shows up in the real world

blocks.content: ["AWS IAM roles and policies are RBAC in production at massive scale. You attach policies, which are permission bundles, to roles, and assign roles to users or services.","Kubernetes RBAC controls exactly who can do what to which cluster resources, like who can read pod logs versus who can delete a namespace.","Enterprise SaaS admin panels almost universally ship an Admin, Member, Viewer style setup, sometimes with custom roles for larger customers."]
items: AWS IAM roles and policies are RBAC in production at massive scale. You attach policies, which are permission bundles, to roles, and assign roles to users or services.
Kubernetes RBAC controls exactly who can do what to which cluster resources, like who can read pod logs versus who can delete a namespace.
Enterprise SaaS admin panels almost universally ship an Admin, Member, Viewer style setup, sometimes with custom roles for larger customers.

blocks.content: If you've ever set up an IAM role in AWS or seen a Kubernetes RoleBinding, you've already used RBAC directly, even if nobody called it that at the time.
8. Worked example: a project management tool
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: a project management tool

blocks.content: Let's design RBAC for something concrete: a Trello style project management tool with three roles.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366501-167641206.png
blocks.alt: Admin, Editor, and Viewer roles each granting a different set of project management permissions

blocks.content: {"headers":["Role","Permissions granted"],"rows":[["Admin","create_task, edit_task, delete_task, invite_member, remove_member, delete_project"],["Editor","create_task, edit_task, comment_task"],["Viewer","view_task, comment_task"]]}
Notice Editor and Viewer both include comment_task. That single permission belongs to two different roles at once, which is exactly the many to many relationship from section 3.
8.1 Checking a permission in code
At request time, the actual check is simple: look up the user's roles, collect the permissions those roles grant, and see if the needed permission is in that set.

blocks.title: Cache the permission set
blocks.content: Recomputing a user's full permission set on every request is fine at small scale. At larger scale, cache it per session or per token and invalidate the cache when role assignments change, otherwise every request pays for a join across three tables.
9. The interview angle

The moment a system design question mentions multiple user types with different permissions, admins, moderators, regular users, guests, RBAC is the expected building block. Interviewers want to see you reach for roles and permission bundles instead of hardcoding a bunch of if user.type === 'admin' checks scattered through the codebase.

["Mention the three core entities: users, roles, permissions, and their many to many relationships.","Bring up role hierarchies if the system has an obvious seniority structure.","Note that you'd enforce checks server side, never trust a role claim from the client alone.","If asked about anything more dynamic like time based or ownership based access, that's your cue to mention ABAC as the natural next step."]
items: Mention the three core entities: users, roles, permissions, and their many to many relationships.
Bring up role hierarchies if the system has an obvious seniority structure.
Note that you'd enforce checks server side, never trust a role claim from the client alone.
If asked about anything more dynamic like time based or ownership based access, that's your cue to mention ABAC as the natural next step.

blocks.content: 10. Summary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396366502-447502335.png
blocks.alt: Managing roles leading to scale and easy auditing

blocks.content: RBAC's whole value is turning an unmanageable pile of individual permission grants into a small, auditable set of roles. Assign users to roles, let roles bundle permissions, and let hierarchies avoid duplicate definitions.

["Direct user to permission grants do not scale past a handful of users.","Roles bundle permissions so managing access means managing role membership.","Users to roles and roles to permissions are both many to many relationships.","Hierarchies let senior roles inherit junior role permissions without duplication.","ABAC is the more flexible, more complex alternative for dynamic, attribute based access.","Least privilege is the philosophy underneath every well designed role.","It's a standard expected answer whenever a design has multiple user types with different access levels."]
items: Direct user to permission grants do not scale past a handful of users.
Roles bundle permissions so managing access means managing role membership.
Users to roles and roles to permissions are both many to many relationships.
Hierarchies let senior roles inherit junior role permissions without duplication.
ABAC is the more flexible, more complex alternative for dynamic, attribute based access.
Least privilege is the philosophy underneath every well designed role.
It's a standard expected answer whenever a design has multiple user types with different access levels.
